title: Autonomy rules are not service
summary: A technology-readiness map connecting federal AV policy, proposed oversight, crash reporting, recalls, powered-lift rules, pilot selections, certification, local infrastructure, and operating service.
map_question: How do mobility and aviation policy records become certified, locally authorized, safety-evidenced autonomous service?
interpretation_boundary: This map connects regulations, proposals, reporting, recalls, and pilot selections. It does not prove aircraft or vehicle certification, operator approval, local permission, comparative safety, completed service, or scale.

nodes.label: Federal policy and program design
nodes.note: The AV Framework and AV STEP proposal define possible federal directions without proving final implementation.

nodes.label: Crash reporting and defect evidence
nodes.note: NHTSA's amended SGO supplies a reporting rail with explicit data limitations.

nodes.label: Weather-related ADS recall
nodes.note: A specific recall exposes software, map, weather, operating-scope, and remedy dependencies.

nodes.label: Powered-lift operating rule
nodes.note: FAA has completed one pilot and operating-rule layer while aircraft and operator approvals remain separate.

nodes.label: eVTOL pilot selections
nodes.note: Eight selected proposals create a test lane but do not establish sites, flights, safety results, or service.

nodes.label: Vehicle, aircraft, and operator approval
nodes.note: Type, production, exemption, operator, route, and operational-design-domain approvals remain system-specific.

nodes.label: Local infrastructure and permission
nodes.note: FTFN still needs sites, roads, airspace, vertiports, charging, emergency processes, insurance, weather, noise, and community records.

nodes.label: Operating service and outcomes
nodes.note: Flights or trips, availability, safety, disruptions, costs, ridership, service area, and enforcement establish operation and scale.

links.note: Policy direction becomes operational through named final rules and approval decisions.
Safety reporting can inform oversight but cannot alone establish a certification or comparative safety finding.
The recall is a regulator-visible defect and remedy record for a specific ADS.
The operating rule leaves aircraft and operator approvals as distinct gates.
Selected pilots still require agreements, approved systems, sites, and test plans.
Federal approval does not replace named local infrastructure, authority, and operating conditions.
Service requires executed local systems and operating records.

what_this_map_supports: Mobility and aviation autonomy can be tracked through policy, rule, reporting, defect, pilot, certification, local-system, and service stages.
A final operating rule and a pilot selection are useful evidence without being treated as certification or service.
Specific recall evidence can expose operating-design-domain dependencies without supporting fleet-wide rankings.
what_this_map_does_not_prove: It does not prove comparative safety, certification, local permission, route viability, service availability, public acceptance, or scale.
It does not treat road ADS and powered-lift aviation as the same regulatory system.
next_records_needed: final AV STEP disposition and AV Framework rulemakings.
